7.4.2 Continuous distributions
A continuous random variable has too many possible outcomes to list in a table, so its distribution takes a different form — one we have already met. When we summarized observed prices and wages, the density curve told us where data were thick and where they were thin, and the area under the curve over any interval gave the proportion of observations falling in that interval. A continuous probability distribution is described by exactly such a curve.

Definition 7.6: Probability density function
A probability density function (PDF) assigns probabilities to intervals of possible outcomes for a continuous random variable. The probability assigned to an interval is the area under the curve over that interval. The curve is never negative, and the total area beneath it is one.


Figure 7.4 shows a density curve for the sale price of a house that will come on the market in one of our three Austin ZIP codes. It’s anchored on our observed data, but that’s not important for now (we’ll talk about how to fit probability models to data soon). The shaded region’s area gives the probability that the sale price lands between $400,000 and $500,000.








Figure 7.4: A probability density function for the sale price of a future home sale in the three-ZIP Austin subset. The shaded area is the probability that the sale price lands between $400,000 and $500,000.





A probability density function is the same kind of object as the density curves of Section 1.2, now describing future data rather than observed data. Under this probability model, the probability that the sale price of any single future house in our three ZIP codes lands between $400,000 and $500,000 is 0.183. Under the frequency interpretation from last chapter: if each of the next 100 sales independently follows this same distribution, we’d expect to see about 18.3% of them selling for a price in that range.






WarningCommon mistake: The height of a density is not a probability



Only areas under a density curve are probabilities; a probability density function can take values greater than one. The curve’s height at $450{,}000 — the middle of the shaded interval — represents the relatively high probability of prices in a small interval around $450{,}000, compared to the probability of seeing a price in an interval of the same width around $150{,}000 or $850{,}000 (for example).



Technical detail 7.2: Why \(\Pr(X \leq x) = \Pr(X < x)\)
For a continuous random variable the two events differ by exactly one value, \(x\), and the region over a single point is a vertical line from \(x\) up to the density curve. A line has no area, so
\[
\Pr(X = x) = 0
\]
for every \(x\), and the two inequalities carry the same probability. This is an abstract mathematical consequence of using an idealized continuous probability distribution; for practical purposes it just means we don’t have to worry about \(\leq\) versus \(<\) (or \(\geq\) versus \(>\)) when we do probability calculations with continuous random variables.



Exercise 7.4: A rectangular density
Suppose a machine’s processing time \(T\), in minutes, has the following probability density. Its graph is a rectangle over the interval from 0 to 0.5 minutes and is zero everywhere else.



Processing time \(t\) (minutes)
Density height \(f(t)\) (per minute)

Check that the total area is one, even though the density height exceeds one.
Find \(\Pr(0.1<T<0.3)\) using the area of a rectangle.
Find \(\Pr(T=0.2)\). Explain why the density height of 2 is not this probability.


Solution
The total area is width times height, \(0.5(2)=1\). Over the interval from 0.1 to 0.3 minutes, the area is \((0.3-0.1)(2)=0.4\), so the interval has probability 0.4. A single point has zero width and hence zero area: \(\Pr(T=0.2)=0\). The density height measures probability per unit of time; probability comes from the area over an interval.



Plotting the accumulated area under the density against the threshold \(x\) traces the CDF, the model analogue of the empirical CDF we drew for observed prices in the first chapter.

Definition 7.7: Cumulative distribution function
The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a random variable gives \(\Pr(X \leq x)\) — the probability accumulated up to the threshold \(x\) — for every possible threshold \(x\). It starts at 0 on the far left and rises to 1 on the far right. Every random variable has a CDF, whether it is discrete, continuous, or a mixture of the two, while a density function exists only for continuous variables. For a discrete random variable the CDF is a step function that jumps at each possible outcome, and the height of the jump is that outcome’s probability.


The relationship runs both ways: the density at \(x\) is the rate at which cumulative probability accumulates as the threshold passes \(x\) (if you’ve had calculus: the PDF is the derivative of the CDF). Figure 7.5 shows the pair for a single threshold ($500K) and probability.








Figure 7.5: Left: the model density with the area below $500,000 shaded. Right: the model’s cumulative distribution function, tracing that accumulated area as the threshold moves. The marked point on the right equals the shaded area on the left.





Varying the threshold traces out the CDF:

title: 7  Probability Basics
text:
Additional practice

Exercise 7.5: Overlapping marketing channels
For one customer, a retailer’s model assigns probability 0.42 to opening an email promotion, 0.28 to viewing the matching social-media promotion, and 0.15 to doing both. Find the probability that the customer sees at least one of the promotions. Then find the probability that the customer sees neither.

Solution
The probability of at least one exposure is
\[
0.42+0.28-0.15=0.55.
\]
The complement rule gives a probability of \(1-0.55=0.45\) that the customer sees neither promotion.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.1 The mean of a random variable
The introduction to this part defined a parameter as a feature of a probability distribution. The mean, median, standard deviation, and quantiles we computed on columns of data all have exact counterparts computed on probability distributions. The formulas look almost the same. The only real change is what gets averaged: instead of summing over observations we have, we sum over outcomes that could happen, each weighted by its probability.
Compare this to the sample mean we computed in Section 3.1, which adds up the observed values and gives each one weight \(1/n\). We can think of that as an expected value too, with respect to a probability distribution that puts probability \(1/n\) on each observed value. When the data contain ties — as for a binary variable like our default indicator — we can collapse the sample mean to a weighted average of the distinct observed values, which looks even more like the formula above.
As a simple first example consider the outcome of a single fair coin toss. Let \(H = 1\) if the coin lands heads and \(H = 0\) otherwise, so \(E[H] = 0.5 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 0 = 0.5\). At first blush this looks odd — the random variable only takes the values zero or one, so what does it mean to expect a value we can’t see? Well, imagine flipping that coin many times over, say 1,000 times. The average of your thousand 0s and 1s will land very close to 0.5. Flip the coin for long enough and the average outcome will get arbitrarily close to 0.5.
A slightly less abstract example: The default indicator \(D\) for a new small-business loan has \(E[D] = 0.75 \times 0 + 0.25 \times 1 = 0.25\) — the expected value of any 0/1 random variable is just the probability of a 1, the model version of the proportion-is-a-mean fact from Section 5.4. In the long run, we expect about 25% of small-business loans to fail under this model.
A similar calculation gives the expected payoff \(E[X]\) on the $10,000 loan at 12% interest:
Table 8.1: Computing the expected payoff of a $10,000 small-business loan at 12% interest. Each row multiplies an outcome by its probability; the expected value is the sum.






Outcome
Probability
Probability × outcome




Repaid: $11,200
0.75
$8,400


Default: $6,000
0.25
$1,500


Expected value

$9,900
The lender expects to collect $9,900 per loan, in the long-run-average sense: if we could fund many independent loans with this profile, the average payoff per loan will settle near $9,900. Whether that is good news depends on what the loan cost. Subtracting the $10,000 principal turns payoffs into profits — a gain of $1,200 if repaid, a loss of $4,000 if not — and the expected profit is the expected payoff minus the principal: $9,900 \(-\) $10,000 = -$100. At 12% interest, this loan loses $100 on average. A lender who funds 100 independent loans like it should expect to end up about $10,000 in the hole.
At 16% interest instead, the payoff when repaid becomes $11,600, the expected payoff rises to $10,200, and the expected profit is now a positive $200 per loan. How far an actual portfolio might stray from that expectation is a question we’ll answer precisely when we combine random variables later in the course. It would be a bad idea in the long run to write loans where we expect to lose money.
For one more example, let’s revisit the FedWatch target-range probabilities from Section 6.1 and Section 7.4. The probability distributions over target ranges after the July and September meetings are:
Weighting midpoints by probabilities gives an implied expected target-range midpoint of 3.685% after the July meeting and 3.815% after September.
The expected increases over the current midpoint of 3.625% are 0.060 and 0.190 percentage points — about 6 and 19 basis points, in the units rate-watchers use (one basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point).

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
Definition 8.1: Mean (expected value) of a random variable
The mean of a random variable, also called its expected value, is a weighted average of its possible outcomes, with each outcome weighted by its probability. For a discrete random variable \(X\) with possible outcomes \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k\),
\[
E[X] = \Pr(X = x_1)\,x_1 + \dots + \Pr(X = x_k)\,x_k
     = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Pr(X = x_i)\,x_i.
\]
We often write \(\mu\) for it: \(E[X] = \mu\). The expected value is the long-run average outcome when the random process repeats many times.










Exercise 8.1: Expected warranty cost
Let \(W\) be the seller’s one-year warranty cost for one appliance. The possible costs are $0 with probability 0.82, $120 with probability 0.15, and $600 with probability 0.03.

Compute the expected warranty cost per appliance.
Explain why no individual appliance has the expected warranty cost, even though the expected value is useful for budgeting across many appliances.


Solution
The expected cost is
\[
E[W]=0.82(0)+0.15(120)+0.03(600)=\$36.
\]
An individual warranty costs $0, $120, or $600, so none costs $36. Across many appliances, however, the average warranty cost per appliance should land near $36 if the model continues to describe the outcomes well.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.2 Variance and standard deviation
Like the sample variance computed with observed data, the variance of a random variable measures the average squared deviation from the mean. As with the mean, the average is weighted by each outcome’s probability.

Definition 8.2: Variance and standard deviation of a random variable
The variance of a random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) is the probability-weighted average of squared deviations from the mean. For a discrete random variable with possible outcomes \(x_1, \dots, x_k\),
\[
\text{Var}(X) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Pr(X = x_i)\,(x_i - \mu)^2.
\]
We write \(\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(X)\). The standard deviation is its square root, \(SD(X) = \sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\). Just like its sample counterpart, the standard deviation is in the same units as \(X\) and can be interpreted as a typical distance from the mean.


In words: the variance is the expected squared distance between the random variable and its mean — how wrong, on the squared-error scale, we expect to be if we predict \(X\) by \(\mu\). For the 16% loan, the payoff sits $1,400 above its mean of $10,200 when the loan is repaid and $4,200 below it on default, so
\[
\text{Var}(X) = 0.75 \times (1{,}400)^2 + 0.25 \times (-4{,}200)^2 = 5{,}880{,}000,
\]
and taking the square root brings us back to dollars: \(SD(X)\) = $2,425. The standard deviation combines the two possible deviations — $1,400 when the loan is repaid and $4,200 when it defaults — into one probability-weighted measure of spread. The interpretation is the one we built for data in Section 3.2: a bigger standard deviation means a less predictable outcome.

Exercise 8.2: Repair time
A repair shop uses this probability distribution for the time \(X\), in hours, needed for a repair:



Repair time \(x\) (hours)
1
2
4




\(\Pr(X=x)\)
0.50
0.30
0.20



Compute the mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(X\). State the units of each result.

Solution
The mean weights each repair time by its probability:
\[
\mu=0.50(1)+0.30(2)+0.20(4)=1.9\text{ hours}.
\]
Weighting the squared deviations from 1.9 gives
\[
\text{Var}(X)=0.50(1-1.9)^2+0.30(2-1.9)^2+0.20(4-1.9)^2
=1.29\text{ hours}^2.
\]
The standard deviation is \(\sqrt{1.29}\approx1.14\) hours. The mean describes the long-run average repair time; the standard deviation measures the spread of repair times around it, in hours rather than squared hours.




Notation 8.1: Random variables, parameters, and statistics

Capital letters name random variables (\(X\), \(Y\), \(D\)).
Lowercase letters name particular values they might take (\(x\), \(y\)).
Greek letters name parameters of a true probability or population distribution: \(\mu\) for its mean, \(\sigma^2\) for its variance, \(\sigma\) for its standard deviation.
Lowercase Latin letters denote quantities computed from a single observed sample: \(\bar{x}\) for a sample mean, \(s^2\) and \(s\) for a sample variance and standard deviation. They are lowercase because they are already-observed numbers, not random.
Uppercase Latin letters like \(\bar X\) denote a quantity computed on a random sample — in this case, the mean of that random sample. They’re random variables because they’re uncertain due to the random sampling. We’ll work with \(\bar X\) when we average random variables later in the course.

When you see a Greek letter, it refers to something unknown we’re trying to estimate. When you see a Latin letter, we have computed it (or could compute it) from data. Lowercase Latin letters (\(\bar{x}\), \(s\)) are numbers we computed from our observed sample; uppercase Latin letters like \(\bar{X}\) are random variables, because the samples they depend on are random.



8.2.1 Variance/Standard deviation measure unpredictability (risk)
As in Section 3.2, the spread of a probability distribution represents unpredictability or risk. The standard deviation is high when there is substantial probability placed on outcomes that are far from the expected value (the mean). Here are two hypothetical $10,000 loans with the same expected profit but different risk profiles. Both assume that the lender recovers $6,000 if the borrower defaults:




Table 8.3: Two loans with the same expected profit and different risk. Loan A charges a higher rate to a riskier borrower; Loan B charges a lower rate to a safer one.












Loan A (riskier borrower, 14%)
Loan B (safer borrower, 8%)




Profit if repaid

$800

-$4,000
-$4,000

$320

$1,440
















Figure 8.1: The two loans’ profit distributions on a common scale, with expected profits marked by dashed lines.











TipInterpretation: standard deviation as unpredictability (risk)



Loan A and Loan B have the same expected profit of $320, so expected value alone cannot choose between them. Their standard deviations can: $2,160 for Loan A against $1,440 for Loan B. Loan A places more probability on outcomes far from that shared average in both directions, which is what a lender means by calling it the riskier loan. Writing many loans like either one is profitable in the long run, provided defaults are close to independent — but a lender choosing between them gets one draw. At the same expected profit, a risk-averse lender takes Loan B.



Exercise 8.3: Equal expected profit, different uncertainty
Project A earns either $0 or $40,000 with equal probability. Project B earns either $15,000 or $25,000 with equal probability.

Compute the mean and standard deviation of each profit distribution.
Why might a manager prefer Project B even though the projects have the same expected profit?


Solution
Both projects have expected profit
\[
0.5(0)+0.5(40{,}000)=0.5(15{,}000)+0.5(25{,}000)=\$20{,}000.
\]
Project A’s outcomes sit $20,000 on either side of the mean, so its standard deviation is $20,000. Project B’s outcomes sit $5,000 on either side, so its standard deviation is $5,000. Project B offers the same expected profit with less uncertainty.



Both loans’ long-run profitability rests on defaults being at least close to independent: one borrower’s failure tells us nothing about the others. We’ll define independence carefully later in the course.
The same comparison drives how investors think about other investments. Two stocks can have return distributions with the same expected return but very different standard deviations; Figure 8.2 shows such a pair.








Figure 8.2: Return distributions for two hypothetical stocks with the same expected return.





You might be happy to hold the more volatile stock in your 401k if you’re young, but the less time you have left to let your portfolio grow, the less attractive this option becomes.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.3 Quantiles and the IQR
Percentiles and quantiles carry over from data to distributions the same way. The \(p\)-th quantile of a distribution is the smallest value where the cumulative probability reaches or exceeds \(p\). For example: the median of a distribution is its 0.5 quantile: the smallest value where the cumulative probability reaches or exceeds 0.50. For our house price model, the median is $488,127:








Figure 8.3: The median of the Austin price model. Left: the density with exactly half its area shaded, up to the median. Right: the CDF crossing cumulative probability 0.50 at the same price.





Just as we discussed in Section 3.1, the median can be a more robust measure of center than the mean for a skewed probability distribution; in the model above, the mean price is $546,458, which is $58,331 above the median. The mean is pulled up by the long right tail of the distribution, just as it was in the observed data.
For a continuous distribution, we can read it off the CDF by finding where the curve crosses height \(p\). The median is the 0.5 quantile, and the interquartile range is the distance between the 0.25 and 0.75 quantiles, a spread measure in the units of the variable that ignores the tails entirely.








Figure 8.4: Reading quantiles off the CDF of the Austin price model. Horizontal lines at cumulative probabilities 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 cross the curve above the model’s quartiles and median; the distance between the two outer drop-lines is the IQR.





For the price model, the quartiles land at $354,282 and $672,536, so the IQR is $318,254: under this model, the middle half of future sales falls in a band about $318,254 wide. Quantiles also answer tail questions directly — a seller wondering “what price will I beat with probability 0.75?” wants the 0.25 quantile, not the mean.

Exercise 8.4: Quantiles for staffing
A call center’s model for next-hour call volume assigns probabilities 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.20, and 0.05 to 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 calls.

Find the median, first quartile, third quartile, and IQR.
If managers want enough staff for at least 75% of hours, which call-volume threshold should they use?


Solution
The cumulative probabilities at 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 calls are 0.10, 0.35, 0.75, 0.95, and 1. The first quartile is 30 calls, the median is 40 calls, and the third quartile is 40 calls. The IQR is therefore \(40-30=10\) calls.
The smallest threshold whose cumulative probability reaches at least 0.75 is 40 calls, so that staffing level covers at least 75% of modeled hours.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.4 Shifting and scaling
Linear transformations of random variables act just like linear transformations applied to columns in our datasets:






NoteMean, median, and standard deviation of \(aX + b\)



If \(X\) is a random variable with mean \(E[X] = \mu\) and standard deviation \(SD(X) = \sigma\), and \(a\) and \(b\) are known constants, then \(Y = aX + b\) has
\[
E[Y] = a\,\mu + b, \qquad \text{median}(Y) = a\,\text{median}(X) + b,
\]
\[
SD(Y) = |a|\,\sigma, \qquad Var(Y) = a^2\,\sigma^2.
\]
Adding \(b\) shifts the center and leaves the spread alone; multiplying by \(a\) scales both the center and the spread (and the spread doesn’t care about the sign of \(a\)).


These are exactly the same rules we encountered for the sample mean, median, and variance/SD in Section 4.1.
The profit on our 16% loan is \(X - 10{,}000\), so its mean is $10,200 \(-\) $10,000 = $200 and its standard deviation is exactly the payoff’s $2,424.87 — shifting can’t make an uncertain payoff any more or less predictable. Scaling Loan B’s $10,000 principal up to $100,000 sets \(a = 10\): expected profit rises to $3,200, and the standard deviation rises right along with it to $14,400.

Exercise 8.5: Warranty pricing
Return to the warranty cost \(W\) from the earlier warranty exercise. A service contract covers that cost and adds $18 in administrative cost, so the seller’s total cost for one contract is \(C=W+18\).

Use the earlier expected value to compute \(E[C]\).
What is the smallest whole-dollar contract price that gives the seller nonnegative expected profit?
What is the expected profit at that price?


Solution
Adding the fixed administrative cost shifts the expected cost:
\[
E[C]=E[W]+18=36+18=\$54.
\]
A $54 price gives expected profit \(54-54=\$0\), so $54 is the smallest whole-dollar price with nonnegative expected profit.




Exercise 8.6: Convert revenue and subtract a fixed fee
A European contract’s revenue \(X\) has mean €120,000 and standard deviation €20,000. At a fixed exchange rate of $1.10 per euro, net dollar revenue is \(Y=1.10X-5{,}000\) after a fixed legal fee.

Find the mean, variance, and standard deviation of \(Y\).
Which part of the transformation changes the spread, and by what factor?


Solution
The transformed mean is
\[
E[Y]=1.10(120{,}000)-5{,}000=\$127{,}000.
\]
The variance and standard deviation are
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=1.10^2(20{,}000^2)=484{,}000{,}000
\]
and
\[
SD(Y)=1.10(20{,}000)=\$22{,}000.
\]
Multiplication by 1.10 scales the standard deviation by 1.10 and the variance by \(1.10^2\). Subtracting the fixed $5,000 fee shifts the center but does not change the spread.



We standardize a random variable by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation, producing a new random variable with mean 0 and standard deviation 1:
\[
Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}.
\]
The new random variable \(Z\) measures how many standard deviations \(X\) sits from its own mean. A realized value of \(Z\) is a z-score and just like in Section 4.2 it measures the size of an observed difference relative to a typical difference, as measured by standard deviation.

title: 8  Measures of Location and Spread (and Other Parameters of Probability Distributions)
text:
8.5 Continuous random variables
The expected value, variance, and standard deviation are all interpreted the same way for a continuous random variable, but the formulas change from sums to integrals:

Technical detail 8.1: Mean and variance as integrals
If a continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x)\) then
\[
E[X] = \int x \, f(x) \, dx, \qquad
\text{Var}(X) = \int (x - \mu)^2 \, f(x) \, dx,
\]
and \(SD(X) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)}\) as always. The integrals play the role the sums played for discrete random variables: they average over every possible outcome, weighting by the density instead of by individual probabilities. The mean and variance of the Austin price model come from integrals of exactly this kind, and software evaluates them.


The mean is still the long-run average, and the standard deviation still measures how far outcomes typically stray from it. The Austin price model’s standard deviation is the square root of its variance, while its median and quartiles come from the CDF.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.1 The probability density function
This chapter introduces one of the most important families of continuous probability distributions: the normal distribution.
A normal distribution’s density is the symmetric bell-shaped curve in Figure 9.1. Changing \(\mu\) slides the curve left or right without altering its shape; changing \(\sigma^2\) stretches or squeezes it without moving the center.
Figure 9.1: Three normal densities. Increasing the mean from 0 to 2 slides the density to the right without changing its shape; increasing the variance from 1 to 4 spreads it out without moving its center.
Since the normal distribution is symmetric, its mean and median are the same.
A shifted and scaled normal random variable is still normal: if \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then \(Y = aX + b\) follows another normal distribution with mean and variance given by the shifting-and-scaling rules from Section 8.4: \(N(a\mu + b,\; a^2\sigma^2)\).

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
Definition 9.1: Normal distribution
The normal distribution (also known as the Gaussian distribution) is the symmetric continuous distribution governed entirely by two parameters: a mean \(\mu\) and a variance \(\sigma^2\). The mean locates the center of the density curve and the variance controls how wide it is.

Details and formulas
The density is
\[
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}
       \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).
\]
The exponent is a squared z-score, so the density falls off with the square of the distance from \(\mu\) measured in standard deviations, and the leading constant is whatever makes the total area equal one. We never evaluate this by hand — software computes normal densities, probabilities, and quantiles.







Notation 9.1: \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
We write
\[
X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)
\]
to say that the random variable \(X\) follows a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\); the “\(\sim\)” reads “is distributed as.”
The second parameter is the variance, not the standard deviation. Most software for computing normal probabilities, densities, and quantiles takes the mean and standard deviation as arguments instead, so the two conventions have to be kept straight when moving between a written model and code.



Exercise 9.1: Reading a normal model
A distribution center models next week’s demand for a product as
\[
X \sim N(500, 80^2),
\]
where \(X\) is measured in units. State the mean, variance, and standard deviation, including units. Which two values would you supply to software that asks for the mean and standard deviation?

Solution
The mean is 500 units, the variance is \(80^2 = 6{,}400\) units squared, and the standard deviation is 80 units. Software that asks for a mean and standard deviation should receive 500 and 80, not 500 and 6,400.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.2 Computing probabilities
To illustrate probability computations with the normal distribution we’ll build a model for weekly S&P 500 returns, using the historical mean and standard deviation as the parameters: \(R \sim N(0.0047, 0.0212^2)\) — a mean weekly return of about 0.47% and a standard deviation of about 2.12%. Figure 9.2 plots the estimated model over the data.








Figure 9.2: Weekly S&P 500 returns (density-scaled histogram) with the fitted normal model overlaid. The fitted density tracks the data well through the middle; the most extreme weeks sit a little further out than the model expects.





Weekly returns are not literally normal — a return can’t fall below \(-100\%\), and real markets tend to produce more extreme outcomes than a normal distribution would give. We are using the normal distribution as an approximation in the region where we want to compute probabilities. We’ll check that approximation against the data below.

Exercise 9.2: Which normal model is most plausible?
A consultant proposes a normal model for each of the following variables:

A calibrated filling machine produces packages whose weights vary around a target.
Annual insurance claim cost per customer is zero for many customers and very large for a few.
A firm measures the percentage of its customers who renew their contracts next year.

For each variable, identify a feature that supports or undermines a normal model. Which variable is most plausibly modeled as normal without a transformation?

Solution
Package weight is continuous and may fluctuate roughly symmetrically around a machine’s target, so it is the most plausible candidate. Annual claim cost has a pile of observations at zero and a long right tail, which conflicts with a normal model. A renewal percentage is bounded between 0% and 100%; a normal approximation could be reasonable if its center is far from both bounds and its spread is small, but the bounds can otherwise matter.



With that model in hand we can compute any probabilities of interest as areas under the curve.

A losing week. \(\Pr(R < 0) = 0.41\). Even in a market that drifts upward on average, the model gives roughly a 41% chance that any given week loses money.
A bad week. \(\Pr(R < -3\%) = 0.05\) — about one week in every 20.
A quiet week. \(\Pr(-1.5\% < R < 1.5\%) = 0.51\).









Figure 9.3: Four probability statements as areas under the fitted normal model for weekly returns. Each panel’s title reports the probability; the shaded region is the corresponding area.





The complement rule gives the probability of a non-losing week:

A non-losing week. \(\Pr(R \geq 0) = 0.59 = 1-\Pr(R < 0)\).
A winning week. \(\Pr(R > 0) = \Pr(R \geq 0)\), because for a continuous distribution, \(\Pr(R = 0) = 0\) and \(\Pr(R \geq 0) = \Pr(R > 0) + \Pr(R = 0)\) since the two events are mutually exclusive.

Software evaluates the normal CDF, and our probability rules let us combine those areas. The same approach works with the CDF of any continuous distribution. If you are unsure which areas to add or subtract, a sketch can help you identify them.
For example, the interval probability \(\Pr(-1.5\% < R < 1.5\%)\) can be computed a few different ways: We can start by computing \(\Pr(R < 1.5\%)\) and then subtracting off \(\Pr(R < -1.5\%)\) to eliminate the tail area we didn’t want. Or we could recognize that \(\Pr(-1.5\% < R < 1.5\%) = 1 - [\Pr(R < -1.5\%) + \Pr(R > 1.5\%)]\), since \(R<-1.5\%\) and \(R>1.5\%\) are the two mutually exclusive ways to land outside the interval. Figure 9.4 sketches both routes.








Figure 9.4: Two routes to the same interval probability. Top row: start with everything below 1.5% and subtract the tail below -1.5%. Bottom row: start with total probability 1 and subtract the two tails outside the interval.






Exercise 9.3: Service-time probabilities
A logistics team models delivery time within a city as \(T \sim N(42, 9^2)\) minutes. For each probability, first sketch the relevant area under a normal curve and then calculate it.

What is the probability that a delivery takes more than 60 minutes?
What is the probability that a delivery takes between 35 and 50 minutes?


Solution
For the first probability, shade the area to the right of 60. Subtract the normal CDF at 60 from one:
\[
\Pr(T>60)=1-\Pr(T\leq 60)\approx 0.0228.
\]
For the second, shade the area between 35 and 50 and subtract the two CDF values:
\[
\Pr(35<T<50)
=\Pr(T<50)-\Pr(T<35)
\approx 0.5946.
\]

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.3 The 68/95/99.7 rule
For normal distributions, three particular areas come up over and over: the probability that an outcome lands within one, two, or three standard deviations of the mean.

Definition 9.2: The 68/95/99.7 rule
If \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then approximately:

68% of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean, \(\mu \pm \sigma\).
95% lies within two standard deviations, \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\).
99.7% lies within three standard deviations, \(\mu \pm 3\sigma\).











Figure 9.5: The 68/95/99.7 rule on the weekly-returns model. Each horizontal bar spans the interval mu plus-or-minus 1, 2, or 3 standard deviations; the label above each bar is the proportion of outcomes landing inside that interval.





Applied to the returns model: about two weeks in three land between -1.6% and 2.6%; about 19 weeks in 20 land between -3.8% and 4.7%; and a week outside -5.9% to 6.8% should be a once-in-several-years event. We can also use the rule to assess a particular return: a \(-4\%\) week sits about two standard deviations below the mean, the kind of week you should expect about once a year (if there’s no dependence between consecutive weekly returns).

Exercise 9.4: Applying the 68/95/99.7 rule
A filling machine produces bottles with a mean fill of 355 milliliters and a standard deviation of 3 milliliters. Assume fill amounts are normally distributed.

Give the intervals containing approximately 68%, 95%, and 99.7% of fills.
A bottle contains 346 milliliters. How many standard deviations below the mean is it?
Approximately what percentage of bottles are at least that far from the mean in either direction?


Solution
The three intervals are 352 to 358 milliliters, 349 to 361 milliliters, and 346 to 364 milliliters. For the 346-milliliter bottle,
\[
z=\frac{346-355}{3}=-3.
\]
It is three standard deviations below the mean. The 68/95/99.7 rule places about 99.7% of bottles within three standard deviations, so approximately 0.3% are at least that far from the mean in either direction.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.4 Z-scores, again
Standardizing a normal random variable — \(Z = (X - \mu)/\sigma\) — produces the standard normal distribution \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\). Since \(Z\) now represents standard deviations from the mean, we know that if a random variable is normally distributed, we should see values more than 2 standard deviations from the mean about 5% of the time, and values more than 3 standard deviations from the mean about 0.3% of the time.






WarningCommon mistake: A z-score alone does not tell you a probability



For any distribution with a finite mean and standard deviation, a z-score tells us how many standard deviations an outcome is from the mean. How unusual that distance is depends on the distribution’s shape. The two distributions in Figure 9.6 both have mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so an outcome of 2.5 has the same z-score in either distribution. We shade the areas beyond \(-2.5\) and \(2.5\) to compare how often outcomes fall at least that far from the mean.










Figure 9.6: Both distributions have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. The shaded areas beyond −2.5 and 2.5 contain about 1.24% of outcomes for the normal distribution and 2.27% for the other distribution. The right panel enlarges the right tail; the left tails are mirror images.






Exercise 9.5: What a z-score does—and does not—tell us
Suppose a strongly right-skewed measure of engineering productivity has a mean of 420 and a standard deviation of 500. One engineer’s observed value is 1,420.

Calculate the z-score and interpret it.
Can you use a normal probability table or normal-distribution software to determine the probability of observing a value at least this large? Explain.


Solution
The z-score is
\[
z=\frac{1{,}420-420}{500}=2.
\]
The observed productivity is two standard deviations above the mean. That interpretation is valid for any distribution. A normal tail probability is not justified, however, because the distribution is strongly right-skewed rather than normal. The z-score alone does not determine a probability.




9.4.1 Finding a normal percentile
A lower-tail probability calculation starts with a threshold and finds the area below it. A quantile calculation reverses this: we specify the area and find the threshold. The 90th percentile of delivery time, for example, is the time by which the model predicts 90% of deliveries will arrive.
Software finds the standard-normal value with the requested area to its left. For an area of 0.90, it gives \(z\approx1.2816\), meaning \(\Pr(Z\leq1.2816)\approx0.90\). To convert back to the original units, rearrange \(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\) to get \(x=\mu+\sigma z\).
For the earlier delivery model \(T\sim N(42,9^2)\) minutes, the 90th percentile is
\[
42+9(1.2816)\approx53.53\text{ minutes}.
\]
About 90% of deliveries take at most 53.53 minutes under this model, and about 10% take longer. For an upper-tail requirement, subtract that tail probability from one before finding the quantile: a threshold exceeded by 10% of deliveries is the 90th percentile.

Exercise 9.6: Fill-volume thresholds
A filling machine’s output follows \(X\sim N(500,4^2)\) milliliters. The table gives standard-normal quantiles computed by software.



Probability to the left
Standard-normal quantile \(z\)




0.20
−0.8416


0.95
1.6449




Find the 20th percentile of fill volume and interpret it.
Find the volume exceeded by 5% of fills. State the probability to the left of this threshold before computing it.


Solution
The 20th percentile is \(500+4(-0.8416)\approx496.63\) milliliters. Under the model, about 20% of fills contain at most this volume.
A threshold with 0.05 above it has \(1-0.05=0.95\) below it, so we use the 95th-percentile quantile. The volume is \(500+4(1.6449)\approx506.58\) milliliters; about 5% of fills exceed it.



The z-score restatement also gives us a quick model check. If weekly returns really follow our fitted normal, about 5% of weeks — five or so out of our 104 — should land more than two standard deviations from the mean. In the data, 6 weeks do: right in line. A handful of weeks land quite far out in the tails, and the tails are exactly where financial data tend to deviate from a normal model. The count checks how often returns exceed one threshold. The QQ plots in the next section compare observed and normal-model quantiles across the distribution; they can also compare quantiles from other distributions.

title: 9  The Normal Distribution
text:
9.5 QQ plots: checking normality
In the last section we checked the returns model at a single quantile, counting the weeks that landed more than two standard deviations from the mean. A quantile-quantile (QQ) plot makes that kind of comparison at every quantile at once. If a variable has a normal distribution, after standardization we know the median should be close to zero, the 2.5th percentile should be about -2, the 97.5th percentile about +2, and so on. The QQ plot puts the theoretical normal quantile on the horizontal axis and the corresponding observed quantile on the vertical axis. If the data are truly close to normal, the points will trace out a straight line. Large departures from the line mean normality is questionable, and where the points bend away tells you how the data deviate. The examples below show the common patterns.
Figure 9.7 builds the plot up one quantile at a time, using our z-scored weekly returns. Each frame fixes a single percentile and asks where it lands in two distributions: in the data (the blue line, dropped onto the density-scaled histogram at top) and in a standard normal (the purple line, on the standard normal density below). That pair of quantiles — one observed, one theoretical — becomes a single point on the plot at right. Sweeping from the 1st percentile to the 99th plots one point per comparison, and the points trace out the QQ curve.






Figure 9.7: Building a QQ plot for the z-scored weekly returns. Each frame matches one percentile between the data (blue, top) and the standard normal (purple, bottom) and records the pair as a point on the right. The finished curve stays close to the 45-degree line, bending away only at the extreme quantiles.



Figure 9.8 runs four variables through the same comparison, each with its QQ plot beside a histogram of its z-scores.








Figure 9.8: Left column: QQ plots of the z-scored variables against the standard normal, so the reference line is the same 45-degree line in every panel. Right column: histograms of the same z-scores with the standard normal density overlaid. Hourly wages are a random subsample of 5,000 workers; daily electricity demand is the mean hourly DFW load for each day from 2016–2020.





Each panel revisits a distribution whose shape we already know from the data chapters. The market returns track the line closely, with the smallest and largest weeks pulling slightly away from it — the outlying weeks from the last section. In small datasets some variability at extreme quantiles is to be expected, but sustained deviations from the line are suspicious. For reference, here are QQ plots for a few randomly generated datasets of the same size as the S&P 500 data, each drawn from a standard normal distribution:








Figure 9.9: QQ plots for six simulated datasets of the same size as the returns data (n = 104), each drawn exactly from a normal distribution. Even perfectly normal data wobbles around the line at the extreme quantiles; deviations of this size are consistent with sampling variation.





Looking through the other examples, we see sustained deviations from normality. Hourly wages bow high above the line at the top: extreme earners are far larger than any normal distribution would produce — strong right skew. The flat run of identical points at the very top is a survey artifact, not a distributional shape: the largest reported earnings are capped at a common value. Taking logs — the transformation from Chapter 4 — pulls the wage points much closer to the line, but we still see some evidence of heavier tails than expected. Daily electricity demand flattens out at both ends of the line: its extremes are less extreme than a normal’s. The flat stretch of points cutting across the line in the middle of the panel is a different signal — many days pile up at similar loads, suggesting a mode or “shoulder” — and neither feature is consistent with a normal distribution.

10.1 Cross-tabulations and contingency tables
We want to understand the relationship between default risk and loan purpose. That relationship is an important input into the business decision of whether to write a loan and how to set its terms. Which loan purposes have the greatest default risk?
We’ll start with counts, because everything else in this chapter is a count divided by some total.
Fourteen purposes make for a bulky table. We want every calculation in this section small enough to check by hand, so we’ll narrow to the 58,456 loans with three of the more interesting purposes: debt consolidation, home improvement, and small business. Table 10.1 shows their crosstab with loan status.
Table 10.1: Cross-tabulation of loan purpose and final loan status for the three-purpose subset. Each cell counts the loans with that combination of purpose and outcome; the margins recover the one-variable frequency tables.

The interior cells record how the two variables tend to move together.
With two variables there are three different totals we could divide each count by, and each choice answers a different question. Take the cell for small-business loans that charged off. Dividing it by the grand total gives the share of all loans that are small business and charged off:
\[
\frac{822}{58,456} = 0.014.
\]
Dividing the small-business row total — the two cells in that row added together — by the grand total gives the share of all loans that are small business:

\]
The crosstab has everything we need to answer the opening question: which loan purposes have the greatest default risk? To compute the small-business default rate, the only relevant information is about small-business loans, so we ignore the other rows and divide by the small-business loan total rather than the grand total. From the counts in Table 10.1, 822 of the 3,191 small-business loans charged off:
\[
\frac{822}{3,191} = 0.258.

10  Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Distributions

title: 10  Joint, Marginal, and Conditional Distributions
text:
Definition 10.1: Cross-tabulation
A cross-tabulation or “crosstab” — also called a contingency table — counts how many observations fall into each combination of two variables’ categories. It has one row per category of the first variable, one column per category of the second, and a count in every cell. Its margins, the row and column of totals, are the frequency tables for the individual variables.








Definition 10.2: Joint proportion
A joint proportion divides an interior cell of a crosstab by the grand total. It is the share of all observations with that combination of categories. The collection of all the joint proportions is the joint distribution of the two variables.





Definition 10.3: Marginal proportion
A marginal proportion divides a row or column total by the grand total. It gives one category’s share without separating the observations by the other variable. Equivalently, we can add the joint proportions across the corresponding row or column.





Exercise 10.1: Hybrid work: joint and marginal proportions
Recall the Bloom, Han, and Liang hybrid-work experiment from Chapter 7. The researchers assigned Trip.com employees either to work in the office five days a week or to work from home two days a week (Bloom et al. 2024). The table records how many employees in each group stayed at or left the firm:

Find the joint proportion of employees who were assigned to Hybrid WFH and left the firm.
Find the marginal distribution of assigned schedule.
Find the marginal distribution of attrition status.


Solution
The Hybrid WFH/Left cell contains 38 of the 1,612 employees, so its joint proportion is \(38/1612=0.0236\).
The row totals give the marginal distribution of assigned schedule: \(820/1612=0.5087\) for Control and \(792/1612=0.4913\) for Hybrid WFH. The column totals give the marginal distribution of attrition status: \(1515/1612=0.9398\) stayed and \(97/1612=0.0602\) left. Each distribution divides by all 1,612 employees and sums to one.






Definition 10.4: Conditional proportion
A conditional proportion divides a cell by its row or column total rather than the grand total. It is the share in one category of one variable among observations in one category of the other. The conditional proportions across all categories of the variable being summarized form its conditional distribution.
The direction of the conditioning matters. Among small-business loans, the share that charged off is 0.258. Among charged-off loans, the share issued to small businesses is 0.085. Both calculations begin with the same cell but divide by different totals.

Solution

\[
\Pr(\text{Stayed}\mid\text{Control})=\frac{761}{820}=0.9280,
\qquad
\Pr(\text{Left}\mid\text{Control})=\frac{59}{820}=0.0720.
\]
Within the Hybrid WFH group, the corresponding distribution is
\[
\Pr(\text{Stayed}\mid\text{Hybrid WFH})=\frac{754}{792}=0.9520,
\qquad
\Pr(\text{Left}\mid\text{Hybrid WFH})=\frac{38}{792}=0.0480.
\]
Each pair sums to one because every employee in that schedule either stayed or left. Reversing the condition gives
\[
\Pr(\text{Hybrid WFH}\mid\text{Left})=\frac{38}{97}=0.3918.
\]
The two conditional probabilities share the same numerator, 38 employees, but use different denominators. The first conditions on the 97 employees who left; the second conditions on the 792 employees assigned to Hybrid WFH.

10.2 From crosstabs to joint distributions
Counts depend on the overall sample size. Dividing every count by the grand total normalizes the table: the interior cells now sum to one. A proportion and its percentage are the same number — 0.014 is 1.4% — and from here on we’ll write everything as proportions.
Table 10.3 shows the result of dividing every count in Table 10.1 by the grand total, 58,456.

The interior cells are the joint proportions we computed from the count table. The margins are the corresponding one-variable distributions. As we saw above, the marginal proportion of small-business loans is the sum of the two joint proportions in that row:
\[
0.041
+ 0.014
= 0.055.
\]
The fully-paid and charged-off small-business loans together account for 0.055 of all the loans in the table.
The normalized table also gives the conditional proportion. Dividing the joint proportion for “small business and charged off” by the marginal proportion of small-business loans gives the same default rate we computed from counts. Because the table is rounded to three decimals, we carry one extra digit in the calculation:
\[
\frac{0.0141}{0.0546} = 0.258.
\]
A conditional proportion is therefore the joint proportion divided by the marginal proportion of the conditioning variable. Dividing count by count or proportion by proportion gives the same answer because the grand total cancels.
This normalized crosstab is the observed-data version of the joint probability tables in the next section. The same correspondence held for one-variable distributions in Section 7.4: probabilities for future outcomes follow the same structure as proportions in observed data. Here it extends to two variables.

section: 10.3 A probability model for future loans
text:
10.3 A probability model for future loans
So far we have read Table 10.3 as a record of what happened to 58,456 historical loans with these three purposes. If those loans are representative of future loans with the same purposes, the table gives estimated probabilities for a future loan drawn from this restricted population.

Exercise 10.3: From an observed share to a future probability
Suppose a lender records 40 defaults among 200 completed loans with the same three purposes used in this chapter. An analyst computes \(40/200=0.20\).

What does 0.20 describe about these completed loans?
Under what assumption could the analyst use 0.20 as an estimated default probability for a future loan from this three-purpose population?


Solution
The value 0.20 is the observed proportion of the 200 loans that defaulted. It describes those completed loans. To use it as an estimated probability for a future loan, we assume that these historical loans represent the future three-purpose population, including its mix of purposes and default behavior. The observed proportion alone does not establish that assumption.




Definition 10.5: Joint probability distribution
For two discrete random variables, a joint probability distribution assigns a probability to every pair of outcomes. Laid out as a table — one variable in the rows, the other in the columns — it follows the same rules as any probability distribution: every cell is non-negative, and all the cells together sum to one.



Notation 10.1: Loan purpose and default
Let \(P\) code the purpose of a future loan from this restricted population: \(P=1\) for debt consolidation, \(P=2\) for home improvement, and \(P=3\) for small business. The numbers are labels, not quantities; they let us represent a categorical outcome with a numerical random variable. Let \(D\) be the loan’s eventual default indicator.


We will use the historical relative frequencies as a probability model for that loan: the probability assigned to each purpose–outcome pair is its count divided by 58,456. For example,
\[
\Pr(\text{small business and default})
= \Pr(P = 3 \text{ and } D = 1)
= \frac{822}{58,456}
= 0.014.
\]
Dividing each of the six interior counts by 58,456 produces the complete joint distribution in Table 10.4.




Table 10.4: The joint probability distribution of purpose and outcome for a future loan from the three-purpose population, estimated from the historical relative frequencies.






Purpose

The six cells cover every possible purpose–outcome pair in this model, and their probabilities add to 1. This is Rule 2 from Section 7.2: one of these pairs must occur.
Rule 3 lets us add probabilities for mutually exclusive pairs. In this model, a loan can default as a debt-consolidation, home-improvement, or small-business loan, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(D = 1)
&= \Pr(P = 1 \text{ and } D = 1)
+ \Pr(P = 2 \text{ and } D = 1)
+ \Pr(P = 3 \text{ and } D = 1) \\
&= 0.139
+ 0.012
+ 0.014 \\
&= 0.165.
\end{aligned}
\]
The probability of default is therefore the sum of the three joint probabilities in the default column.

Definition 10.6: Marginal probability distribution
A marginal probability distribution gives the probability distribution of one variable on its own. We obtain it from a joint distribution by summing over all possible outcomes of the other variable.


Adding the row and column sums to Table 10.4 gives both marginal distributions.

These one-variable distributions appear in the margins of the joint table, which is where the name marginal comes from. For example, summing the two small-business joint probabilities gives its marginal probability:
\[
\Pr(P = 3)
= 0.041
+ 0.014
= 0.055.
\]
The marginal distribution of \(D\) answers “what is the default probability for a future loan with one of these three purposes before we know which one?” But it deliberately averages over purposes, and we know from Table 10.2 that purpose matters. The sharper question is conditional: given that the loan is for a small business, what is the chance it defaults?

10.3.1 Conditional probability

Definition 10.7: Conditional probability
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(\Pr(B) > 0\), the conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is
\[
\Pr(A \mid B) = \frac{\Pr(A \text{ and } B)}{\Pr(B)}.
\]
The bar “\(\mid\)” reads “given that” or “conditional on.” To condition on \(B\), keep only the probability that is consistent with \(B\) and rescale it so it sums to one again. That is what dividing the joint probability by the marginal probability of \(B\) does.


The formula is exactly the joint-over-marginal arithmetic we did with proportions in Section 10.2, now stated as a definition.
On the table, conditioning is a two-step procedure: keep the row or column consistent with the condition, then renormalize the remaining probabilities by dividing by their total. Conditioning on \(P = 3\) keeps the small-business row. Its total is the marginal probability \(\Pr(P = 3)\). Dividing each joint probability in that row by \(\Pr(P = 3)\) gives the conditional distribution in Table 10.6.

Together, the probabilities 0.742 and 0.258 form the conditional distribution of \(D\) given \(P = 3\). Because this probability model uses the historical relative frequencies, they match the conditional proportions computed from counts in Section 10.1; Section 7.4 rounded the default probability to 0.25 for its introductory example.
Among the three purposes, small-business loans have the largest default probability: \(\Pr(D = 1 \mid P = 3) =
0.258\). This is the relevant comparison when we ask which loan purpose has the greatest default risk.
The reverse conditional answers a different question: among the loans that defaulted, what share were for small businesses?
\[
\Pr(P = 3 \mid D = 1)
= \frac{822}{9,670}
= 0.085.
\]
Small-business loans account for only 0.055 of all loans. Even with the largest default risk, they make up only 0.085 of the defaulted loans.
Most defaulted loans are debt-consolidation loans:
\[
\Pr(P = 1 \mid D = 1)
= \frac{8,131}{9,670}
= 0.841.
\]
Debt-consolidation loans have a lower default probability, \(\Pr(D = 1 \mid P = 1) =
0.165\), but they account for 0.845 of all loans. Their large base rate explains why they also account for most defaults.

\]

For Basic customers, divide the two joint probabilities in the Basic row by the row’s marginal probability, 0.70:
\[
\Pr(\text{Renews}\mid\text{Basic})=\frac{0.42}{0.70}=0.60,
\qquad

\]
For Premium customers, divide by 0.30:
\[
\Pr(\text{Renews}\mid\text{Premium})=\frac{0.24}{0.30}=0.80,
\qquad
\Pr(\text{Does not renew}\mid\text{Premium})=\frac{0.06}{0.30}=0.20.
\]
Among renewing customers, the Premium share is
\[
\Pr(\text{Premium}\mid\text{Renews})=\frac{0.24}{0.66}=0.3636.
\]
The value 0.24 is the joint probability that a customer is Premium and renews. The Premium renewal rate conditions on Premium customers, so it is \(0.24/0.30=0.80\).









WarningReversing the condition changes the denominator



Conditional probabilities are asymmetric. The two share a numerator — the joint probability of \(A\) and \(B\) — but divide it by different base rates (marginal probabilities), so one can be tiny while the other is close to one.


Most tall people aren’t in the NBA, but most people in the NBA are tall: \(\Pr(\text{NBA} \mid \text{tall})\) is minuscule while \(\Pr(\text{tall} \mid \text{NBA})\) is close to one. Mathematically,
\[
\Pr(\text{NBA} \mid \text{tall}) = \frac{\Pr(\text{NBA and tall})}{\Pr(\text{tall})},
\qquad
\Pr(\text{tall} \mid \text{NBA}) = \frac{\Pr(\text{NBA and tall})}{\Pr(\text{NBA})}.
\]
Adult heights are roughly normal, so about half of adults are taller than average. The first conditional therefore divides a tiny joint probability by about 0.5 and stays tiny. The second divides that same joint probability by the much smaller probability of being in the NBA, producing a conditional probability near 1.

title: 11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes’ Rule
text:
11.1 The Fed’s two meetings
CME FedWatch uses futures prices to estimate probabilities for future federal funds target ranges. In the July 9, 2026 snapshot we use here, its model allows a hold or a 25-basis-point hike at each of the next two meetings. A hike of 25 basis points raises the target range by 0.25 percentage points.
On July 9, the target range was 3.50–3.75%. Futures prices implied a probability of 0.2459 that the Fed would hike at its July 29 meeting and a probability of 0.7541 that it would hold. The FedWatch model assigns zero probability to a cut in this snapshot. We can arrange the nearby outcomes in a branching tree:
Figure 11.1: Market-implied probabilities for the July 29 target range, as reported by CME FedWatch on July 9, 2026. The dashed branch shows a nearby move outside the two supported outcomes in this snapshot.
If the Fed were to hike rates at the July meeting, a hold in September would leave the target at 3.75–4.00%, while another hike would raise it to 4.00–4.25%. We reconstruct the conditional branch probabilities from CME’s published target-range probabilities under this model. The probability of a September hike given a July hike is 0.5007:
Figure 11.2: September meeting probabilities after a July hike. Here hold and hike describe the September move; the leaves show the resulting target ranges.
These are conditional probabilities because they answer an “if” question: If the Fed hikes in July, what is the chance of another hike in September? The action on a September branch is a move relative to the July target; the leaf at the end of that branch is the resulting September target range.
If instead the Fed holds the target steady in July, the possible September outcomes start from 3.50–3.75%. The same September move probabilities now lead to different target ranges:
Figure 11.3: September meeting probabilities after a July hold. CME applies the same meeting-level move distribution after either July branch.
A September hold after a July hike also lands at 3.75–4.00%, giving us a second path to that target range.
We can collect these possibilities into one tree representing the different paths the target range could take over the two meetings:
Figure 11.4: The probability tree implied by CME FedWatch’s traditional conditional method. The first branches carry July’s marginal probabilities; the second branches apply September’s meeting-level move probabilities after each July outcome. Dashed branches show nearby moves outside the supported pair.
We omitted the July-cut branch from the full tree because a cut was outside the two moves supported by this snapshot; the dashed September paths remain for reference. The tree is another way to represent a joint probability distribution over the target ranges after the July and September meetings. The probabilities on the branches leaving any one node sum to 1. Its first branches show the marginal distribution for July. The next set of branches applies the September meeting’s move distribution after each July outcome. Together they let us reconstruct the joint distribution and the marginal distribution of the September target range.

11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes' Rule

title: 11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes’ Rule
text:
Technical detail 11.1: How FedWatch constructs the meeting probabilities
FedWatch uses monthly federal funds futures prices to infer the expected change in the effective federal funds rate at each scheduled meeting. It expresses that expected change in 25-basis-point increments, then splits probability between the two adjacent increments that bracket it. For example, an expected 15-basis-point increase becomes a 0.4 probability of a hold and a 0.6 probability of a 25-basis-point hike.
The method does not limit the Fed to a single 25-basis-point move. An expected 72.5-basis-point increase would instead become a 0.1 probability of a 50-basis-point hike and a 0.9 probability of a 75-basis-point hike. Expected decreases produce the corresponding pair of cuts. CME’s methodology gives the complete construction.

11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes' Rule

title: 11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes’ Rule
text:
11.2 Multiplying along a path
Consider the joint probability of two hikes, which corresponds to a 4.00–4.25% target range in September. The probability of a July hike is 0.2459, and given a July hike, the probability of another hike is 0.5007. We defined conditional probability as
\[
\Pr(A \mid B) = \frac{\Pr(A \text{ and } B)}{\Pr(B)}.
\]






NoteThe product rule



For \(\Pr(B)>0\), multiplying both sides by \(\Pr(B)\) gives the product rule:
\[
\Pr(A \text{ and } B) = \Pr(B)\Pr(A \mid B).
\]
A joint probability is the probability of the condition times the probability of the other event given that condition.


The first factor is the probability of reaching the July branch; the second is the probability of the September move given that July outcome. Their product is the probability of the full path. Therefore, the probability of two consecutive hikes is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Pr(\text{July hike and September hike}) \\
&\qquad = \Pr(\text{July hike})
   \Pr(\text{September hike} \mid \text{July hike}) \\
&\qquad = 0.2459 \times 0.5007
\approx 0.1231.
\end{aligned}
\]

Exercise 11.1: A subscription path
Suppose 30% of visitors to a website start a free trial. Among visitors who start a trial, 40% buy a subscription. What is the probability that a randomly selected visitor starts a trial and buys a subscription? Explain why 0.40 alone does not answer this question.

Solution
Multiplying along the path gives \(0.30(0.40)=0.12\). Thus, 12% of all visitors start a trial and buy a subscription. The 0.40 conditions on having started a trial; it describes only the visitors who reach that branch.

title: 11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes’ Rule
text:
11.3 The law of total probability
Now suppose we are interested in the probability that the target range is 3.75–4.00% in September. There are two ways to get there: a hold followed by a hike, or a hike followed by a hold. The two paths are mutually exclusive, so we add their joint probabilities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(\text{September target } 3.75\text{--}4.00\%)
&= \underbrace{0.7541 \times 0.5007}_{
     \substack{\text{hold in July,}\\\text{then hike in September}}}
+ \underbrace{0.2459 \times 0.4993}_{
     \substack{\text{hike in July,}\\\text{then hold in September}}} \\
&\approx 0.3776 + 0.1228 \\
&= 0.5004.
\end{aligned}
\]
This calculation recovers CME’s reported September probability from the two paths that lead to that target range.
The tree highlights both complete paths in dark red, with each path’s probability to the right of its September outcome:








Figure 11.5: The two dark-red paths end at a September target range of 3.75–4.00%. Each path probability is the product of its July probability and its conditional September probability. Values are rounded to four decimals; dashed branches have probability zero.











NoteThe law of total probability



The law of total probability applies the same calculation to any event \(B\). Suppose \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) are mutually exclusive and exhaustive events: exactly one of them occurs. For events \(A_i\) with positive probability,
\[
\Pr(B)=\sum_{i=1}^k \Pr(A_i)\Pr(B\mid A_i).
\]
Each term is the joint probability of \(A_i\) and \(B\). Adding these terms accounts for every way \(B\) can occur, just as summing a column of a joint probability table gives its marginal probability.


Computing the other joint probabilities and summing the rows and columns gives a complete probability table like the one we started with for LendingClub:

The loan table’s conditional default distribution changes across purposes. In the FedWatch construction, the September move distribution stays essentially the same across July branches, even though the resulting September target range depends on July’s target.

Exercise 11.2: Orders ready on time
Suppose a restaurant receives 70% of its takeout orders through its app and 30% by phone. These are its only two ordering methods. It has 90% of app orders and 80% of phone orders ready at the promised time.

Find the probability of each path that ends with an order ready on time.
Find the probability that a randomly selected order is ready on time. Explain why you can add the two path probabilities.


Solution
The app-and-ready path has probability \(0.70(0.90)=0.63\), and the phone-and-ready path has probability \(0.30(0.80)=0.24\). Every order uses exactly one of these methods, so the paths are mutually exclusive and account for every order ready on time. Adding gives \(0.63+0.24=0.87\): 87% of orders are ready at the promised time.

title: 11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes’ Rule
text:
11.4 Worked example: Fraud screening
Suppose an online retailer uses a system that flags transactions for manual review. In our model, 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent. The system flags 95% of fraudulent transactions and 2% of legitimate transactions. Given that the system flags a transaction, what is the probability that it is fraudulent?
Let \(F\) denote the event that a transaction is fraudulent and \(A\) the event that the system flags it. The 95% rate is a share of fraudulent transactions, so it gives \(\Pr(A\mid F)\). Our inputs are
\[
\Pr(F)=0.005,\qquad
\Pr(A\mid F)=0.95,\qquad
\Pr(A\mid F^c)=0.02,
\]
where \(F^c\) means the transaction is legitimate. The question asks for the reverse conditional, \(\Pr(F\mid A)\).
The tree shows the two possible screening outcomes within each transaction status and the probability of each complete path:








Figure 11.6: Fraud-screening probability tree. Multiplying the branch probabilities gives each joint probability on the right. The two flagged paths contribute to the overall probability of a flag.





Fraudulent transactions make up 0.5% of all transactions, and the system flags 95% of that group. Multiplying these two shares gives the joint probability that a transaction is fraudulent and flagged:
\[
\Pr(F\text{ and }A)=0.005\times0.95=0.00475.
\]
A flag can also come from a legitimate transaction. Adding the probabilities of these two paths gives the overall probability of a flag:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A)
&=\Pr(F)\Pr(A\mid F)+\Pr(F^c)\Pr(A\mid F^c)\\
&=0.005\times0.95+0.995\times0.02\\
&=0.00475+0.01990=0.02465.
\end{aligned}
\]
Among flagged transactions, the fraudulent share is therefore
\[
\Pr(F\mid A)
=\frac{\Pr(F\text{ and }A)}{\Pr(A)}
=\frac{0.00475}{0.02465}
\approx0.193.
\]
About 19.3% of flagged transactions are fraudulent. The system catches 95% of fraud, but legitimate transactions are much more common, so even their 2% flag rate produces more flags than the fraudulent transactions do.
We can represent these rates with a hypothetical group of 100,000 transactions. Of the 500 fraudulent transactions, the system flags \(500\times0.95=475\). Of the 99,500 legitimate transactions, it flags \(99{,}500\times0.02=1{,}990\):

title: 11  Probability Trees, Total Probability, and Bayes’ Rule
text:
11.5 Bayes’ rule
The fraud calculation starts with a probability of a flag given fraud and uses it to find the probability of fraud given a flag. Substituting the product rule into the conditional-probability definition gives Bayes’ rule:
\[
\Pr(F\mid A)
=\frac{\Pr(F)\Pr(A\mid F)}{\Pr(A)}.
\]
The numerator is the probability of a fraudulent transaction that produces a flag. Dividing by the probability of a flag restricts the comparison to the flagged transactions, as in the conditional tables in Chapter 10.






NoteBayes’ rule



Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\) be mutually exclusive and exhaustive events with positive probabilities, and suppose \(\Pr(B)>0\). Combining the product rule and the law of total probability gives
\[
\Pr(A_j\mid B)
=\frac{\Pr(A_j)\Pr(B\mid A_j)}
       {\sum_{i=1}^k\Pr(A_i)\Pr(B\mid A_i)}.
\]
We multiply each starting probability \(\Pr(A_i)\) by the conditional probability of the observed event \(B\) within that group. These products are the joint probabilities of each group and \(B\). Dividing by their sum makes the conditional probabilities add to 1, just as we renormalized the selected entries of a joint table in Chapter 10.



Exercise 11.3: The same filter in two inboxes
Suppose an email filter flags 90% of spam messages and 10% of messages that are not spam. These rates are the same in two inboxes. In Inbox A, 10% of incoming messages are spam; in Inbox B, 50% are spam.

For each inbox, find the probability that a message is spam given that the filter flags it.
Explain why these probabilities differ even though the filter has the same flagging rates in both inboxes.


Solution
For Inbox A, the spam-and-flagged path has probability \(0.10(0.90)=0.09\), and the nonspam-and-flagged path has probability \(0.90(0.10)=0.09\). The spam share among flagged messages is therefore \(0.09/(0.09+0.09)=0.50\).
For Inbox B, the corresponding path probabilities are \(0.50(0.90)=0.45\) and \(0.50(0.10)=0.05\). The spam share among flagged messages is \(0.45/(0.45+0.05)=0.90\).
Spam is more common among incoming messages in Inbox B, so more of its flags come from spam. Holding the two conditional flagging rates fixed does not hold the composition of flagged messages fixed.




Exercise 11.4: Supplier risk as a probability tree
A buyer orders 60% of its components from Supplier A and 40% from Supplier B. The probability that a component is defective is 0.02 given Supplier A and 0.05 given Supplier B.

Draw a probability tree whose first branches identify the supplier and whose second branches identify whether the component is defective or not defective. Label every branch.
Compute the probability of each of the four paths.
Use the path probabilities to construct the joint probability table of supplier and defect status, including both marginal distributions.
Find the marginal probability that a component is defective.
Given that a component is defective, find the probability that it came from Supplier B.
Explain why the answer to part 5 exceeds the marginal probability of ordering from Supplier B.


Solution
The first branches have probabilities 0.60 for Supplier A and 0.40 for Supplier B. The second-stage branch probabilities are 0.02 Defective and 0.98 Not defective after Supplier A, and 0.05 Defective and 0.95 Not defective after Supplier B. The completed tree is








Figure 11.7: Completed supplier-risk probability tree. The first branches show the marginal supplier probabilities; the second branches show the conditional defect-status probabilities within each supplier.





Multiplying along each path gives the four joint probabilities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(A\text{ and Defective}) &= 0.60(0.02)=0.012, \\
\Pr(A\text{ and Not defective}) &= 0.60(0.98)=0.588, \\
\Pr(B\text{ and Defective}) &= 0.40(0.05)=0.020, \\
\Pr(B\text{ and Not defective}) &= 0.40(0.95)=0.380.
\end{aligned}
\]
The path probabilities and their margins form the joint table:

title: 12  Independence
text:
12.1 Independence
A conditional distribution tells us how the distribution of one variable changes when we learn the value of another. In our running example, once we know a LendingClub loan is for a small business we know it’s more likely to default than average — the new information changes our assessment of how likely a default is.
What would it mean if the chance of default was the same for each loan purpose? Or, put in the language of probability, what would it mean if the conditional distribution of defaults was identical for every loan purpose? Intuitively we would say that the chance a loan defaults doesn’t depend on why the borrower took out the loan — loan purpose and defaults would be independent. If even one conditional distribution differs from its marginal distribution, the variables are dependent. Formally this reduces to the following definition:
The conditional form expresses the idea of unchanged information; the product form gives us a direct check on a joint table. They agree because a conditional probability is the joint probability divided by the probability of the condition. If the joint probability is \(\Pr(X=x)\Pr(Y=y)\), dividing by \(\Pr(Y=y)\) leaves \(\Pr(X=x)\).
Independence works in both directions. The product is unchanged when we swap \(X\) and \(Y\), so independence also gives \(\Pr(Y=y\mid X=x)=\Pr(Y=y)\) whenever \(\Pr(X=x)>0\).
crumbs: Data analysis, visualizations, and probability models for multiple random variables

title: 12  Independence
text:
Definition 12.1: Independent random variables
Two discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if
\[
\Pr(X=x,Y=y)=\Pr(X=x)\Pr(Y=y)
\]
for every pair of outcomes \(x\) and \(y\). That is, each joint probability equals the product of its two marginal probabilities. Equivalently,
\[
\Pr(X=x\mid Y=y)=\Pr(X=x)
\]
for every \(x\) and every \(y\) with \(\Pr(Y=y)>0\). The distribution of \(X\) stays the same whichever value of \(Y\) we learn.










Tip 12.1: Checking independence in a joint table



To establish independence from a joint table, every interior cell must satisfy the product equality in the definition. One failing cell is enough to establish dependence.

12.2 Loan purpose and default
The 58,456 LendingClub loans in our three-purpose subset give us conditional default rates to compare with the overall rate. Table 12.1 reports historical relative frequencies: each rate divides the number of charged-off loans by the number of loans with that purpose.




Table 12.1: Historical default rates for the three-purpose LendingClub subset.

The overall default rate is 16.5%. Knowing that a loan funded a small business raises the historical rate to 25.8%, a difference of 9.3 percentage points. Knowing that it funded home improvement lowers the rate to 12.2%. Purpose changes the default distribution.
If we use these historical relative frequencies as a probability model for a future loan from the same three-purpose population, purpose and default are dependent in that model. The small-business/default cell also fails the product check:
\[
\underbrace{\Pr(\text{small business and default})}_{0.0141}
\ne
\underbrace{\Pr(\text{small business})\Pr(\text{default})}_{0.0090}.
\]
The joint probability exceeds the product because default is more common among small-business loans than overall. The debt-consolidation rate rounds to the same value as the overall rate, but that does not establish independence: the other purposes differ, and the definition requires equality for every outcome. These comparisons describe an association; they do not establish that changing a loan’s stated purpose would change its default risk.

Exercise 12.1: Delivery delays
A retailer’s historical records show that 8% of all deliveries arrived late. Among standard deliveries, 10% arrived late; among express deliveries, 2% arrived late. Treat these historical proportions as the probabilities for a future delivery.

Are delivery service and late arrival independent in this model? Give a numerical comparison that supports your answer.
Find the conditional probability of an on-time arrival given express service, and compare it with the marginal probability of an on-time arrival.


Solution
The variables are dependent because \(\Pr(\text{late}\mid\text{express})=0.02\) differs from \(\Pr(\text{late})=0.08\). The standard-service comparison also fails: \(0.10\ne0.08\). An express delivery arrives on time with conditional probability \(1-0.02=0.98\), compared with the marginal probability \(1-0.08=0.92\). Learning the service changes both probabilities in the arrival-status distribution.

12.3 Target ranges at two Fed meetings
CME FedWatch uses federal funds futures prices to assign market-implied probabilities to future federal funds target ranges. Here we use its July 9, 2026 snapshot for the target range after the July 29 and September 16 Federal Open Market Committee meetings. The supported moves at each meeting in this snapshot are a hold or an increase of 0.25 percentage points.
Those supported moves constrain the combinations of July and September outcomes. A September target of 4.00–4.25% requires July already to have reached 3.75–4.00%; starting September at 3.50–3.75% would require a larger increase than this snapshot supports. Similarly, a July target of 3.75–4.00% cannot be followed by a September target of 3.50–3.75% under these moves. Table 12.2 retains these impossible combinations as zeros. They are constraints of this probability model, not claims about everything the Fed could conceivably do.

WarningSimilar sample proportions do not establish independence



These conditional proportions are nearly unchanged, but they are not exactly equal. Even if employment status and ratings were independent in a population model, random sampling would generally produce some differences among the observed proportions. Conversely, rounding can make two sample proportions look identical even when they differ. This table provides evidence about whether independence might be a useful approximation; it does not establish exact independence in the U.S. adult population.


Independence is an exact property of a probability model. In the website example we specified a mechanism that makes every joint probability equal to its product of margins. For SHED, we observe responses and must judge whether such a model adequately approximates the relationship. The unweighted table alone also does not account for the survey’s sampling design.
